pieces.h: Voltage, current, resistance: the three numbers
pieces.d: Every circuit you will ever meet is a story about three quantities. Learn what each one is and the rest of electronics stops being magic.

pieces.h: Sleep: what it is doing while you are out
pieces.d: You spend a third of your life asleep, and it is not downtime. Knowing the machinery makes the standard advice easier to follow.

pieces.h: How a habit actually forms
pieces.d: A habit is a behaviour your brain has stopped deciding about. Understanding the loop behind it tells you where to push if you want to build one or break one.

pieces.h: Hosting a home game that people come back to
pieces.d: A good home game is smooth, fair and friendly. A little preparation by the host prevents nearly every argument.

pieces.h: Compound interest: the curve that bends
pieces.d: Growth on top of growth looks like nothing for years and then looks like magic. The arithmetic is simple, and time is the ingredient you cannot buy later.

pieces.h: The printing press: when copies became cheap
pieces.d: Around 1450 a goldsmith in Mainz found a way to mass-produce the written word. Within two generations, Europe was a different place.

pieces.h: Ohm's law in your head
pieces.d: One short formula does most of the arithmetic in electronics. Here is how to use it without a calculator and how to know when it stops applying.

pieces.h: Strength training: the short version
pieces.d: Lifting heavy things on purpose is among the best-supported habits for a long and capable life. The principles fit on one page.

pieces.h: If-then plans: the smallest trick that works
pieces.d: Good intentions fail at a predictable point: the moment of action. One sentence, written in advance, moves the decision out of that moment.

pieces.h: Card room etiquette: the unwritten rules
pieces.d: Sitting down in a casino poker room for the first time is intimidating. A dozen conventions, most of them simple courtesy, cover nearly everything.

pieces.h: Index funds: buying the whole haystack
pieces.d: Instead of hunting for the winning stocks, own all of them. It sounds like giving up. Over long periods it has beaten most of the professionals.

pieces.h: Germ theory: the invisible cause
pieces.d: For most of history, nobody knew what made people sick. The discovery that tiny living things cause disease is barely 150 years old.

pieces.h: Power and heat: why parts burn
pieces.d: Voltage and current together make power, and power that has nowhere to go becomes heat. This is the sum that decides whether a part survives.

pieces.h: Cardio: how much, how hard
pieces.d: Your heart and lungs adapt to what you ask of them. The guidelines are modest, the benefits are large, and most of the work should feel easy.

pieces.h: Attention is the scarce thing
pieces.d: You cannot do two demanding things at once, and switching between them costs more than it feels like. Protecting attention is mostly a matter of design.

pieces.h: Pot-limit Omaha in five minutes
pieces.d: Four hole cards instead of two, and a cap on bet size. Omaha looks like hold'em and punishes anyone who plays it that way.

pieces.h: Risk, volatility and why diversification works
pieces.d: Spreading money around is the one move in investing that lowers risk without necessarily lowering return. Here is the mechanism behind the slogan.

pieces.h: Plate tectonics: the ground is moving
pieces.d: The continents drift at the speed your fingernails grow. The idea was ridiculed for half a century before the evidence from the sea floor settled it.

pieces.h: Series and parallel: two ways to connect anything
pieces.d: There are only two basic ways to join parts. Knowing which one you are looking at tells you what the voltage and current must be doing.

pieces.h: Protein: how much you need and why
pieces.d: Protein is the one nutrient your body cannot store for later. The basics of how much, when and from what are simpler than the supplement aisle suggests.

pieces.h: Spaced repetition: remembering on purpose
pieces.d: Forgetting follows a curve. Review something just as it is about to slip and you flatten the curve, with a fraction of the effort cramming takes.

pieces.h: Pot odds: the price of a call
pieces.d: Every call is a purchase. Pot odds tell you the price, and whether the hand you hold is worth paying it.

pieces.h: Inflation: the slow leak in every dollar
pieces.d: Prices rise a little each year, and a little each year becomes a lot over a working life. Understanding the leak changes how you think about saving.

pieces.h: Natural selection in five minutes
pieces.d: The most important idea in biology needs only three ingredients, and none of them involves intention. Here is what it claims and what it does not.

pieces.h: The voltage divider: the most reused circuit there is
pieces.d: Two resistors and one idea. It sets reference levels, reads sensors and shrinks signals, and it hides inside thousands of larger circuits.

pieces.h: Caffeine: how the world's favourite drug works
pieces.d: Most adults take it every day. It does not give you energy. It hides the signal that you are tired, which is useful if you know the rules.

pieces.h: Test yourself: retrieval beats rereading
pieces.d: The most common study method, reading it again, is one of the weakest. Pulling information out of your head teaches you more than putting it back in.

pieces.h: Outs and the rule of 2 and 4
pieces.d: Count the cards that save you, multiply by two or by four, and you have your chance of improving, close enough to act on.

pieces.h: The emergency fund: boring money that buys freedom
pieces.d: A few months of expenses in plain cash earns almost nothing and is still one of the best financial decisions most people can make.

pieces.h: DNA: the molecule that carries instructions
pieces.d: Four chemical letters, arranged along a twisted ladder, hold the plans for every living thing. Here is how that works and how it was found.

pieces.h: AC and DC: why the wall and the battery disagree
pieces.d: Batteries push one way. The wall socket reverses direction many times a second. The reasons are historical, practical and still shaping every gadget you own.

pieces.h: Water: how much you actually need
pieces.d: Eight glasses a day is a rule nobody can trace to solid evidence. Your body already has a precise system for this, and it mostly works.

pieces.h: Procrastination is not about time
pieces.d: Putting things off looks like a planning problem. The research points somewhere else: it is a way of managing a bad feeling, and that changes the fix.

pieces.h: Equity: your share of the pot
pieces.d: Before the last card is dealt, nobody owns the pot. Equity is the share that belongs to you on average, and thinking in shares changes how you play.

pieces.h: Getting out of debt: avalanche, snowball and the minimum trap
pieces.d: There are two well-known orders in which to pay off debts. One is cheaper. The other is easier to stick with. Both beat the default.

pieces.h: The periodic table: a map that predicted the future
pieces.d: A Russian chemistry teacher arranged the known elements on cards and left gaps for ones nobody had found. He was right about the gaps.

pieces.h: Resistors: reading them and choosing them
pieces.d: The cheapest part on the board and the one you will use most. How to read the stripes, pick a value and avoid the three usual mistakes.

pieces.h: Knife skills: the fifteen-minute upgrade
pieces.d: One good knife, held properly and kept sharp, makes cooking faster and safer than a drawer full of gadgets.

pieces.h: Confirmation bias: the mother of all biases
pieces.d: People do not weigh evidence evenly. We look for what agrees with us, and we are far better at spotting flaws in arguments we dislike.

pieces.h: Expected value: the only score that counts
pieces.d: Results tell you what happened. Expected value tells you whether the decision was right. Poker is won by people who learn to tell the two apart.

pieces.h: How a mortgage really works
pieces.d: The monthly payment never changes, but what it buys changes every month. Seeing the schedule explains why early extra payments are so powerful.

pieces.h: Entropy: why time has a direction
pieces.d: Eggs break and do not unbreak. Coffee cools and never reheats itself. One law of physics explains why the film of the world only runs one way.

pieces.h: Capacitors: small tanks for charge
pieces.d: A capacitor stores a little energy and gives it back quickly. That one behaviour smooths power, blocks DC, sets timing and keeps chips alive.

pieces.h: Browning: the chemistry that makes food taste good
pieces.d: The crust on a steak, the colour of toast and the smell of roasting coffee come from the same reaction. Controlling it is the core of savoury cooking.

pieces.h: Anchoring: the first number wins
pieces.d: An arbitrary figure mentioned at the start of a judgement drags the final answer toward itself, even when everyone knows it is meaningless.

pieces.h: Implied odds: the money that is not in the pot yet
pieces.d: Sometimes the price of a call is wrong on paper and right in practice, because of what you stand to win later. Here is when that is true and when it is wishful.

pieces.h: Credit scores: what the number measures
pieces.d: A three-digit number decides what you pay to borrow. It follows a small set of rules, and most of them reward doing boring things for a long time.

pieces.h: Relativity in five minutes
pieces.d: Einstein's two theories changed what space, time and gravity mean. The core ideas can be stated without mathematics, and your phone depends on them.

pieces.h: Inductors: the part that fights change in current
pieces.d: Coil a wire and it gains inertia. Inductors make switching power supplies possible, and their kickback is why relays kill transistors.

pieces.h: Cast iron: care without the superstition
pieces.d: A cast iron pan can outlive its owner and needs less fuss than its reputation suggests. Most of the rules people repeat about it are out of date.

pieces.h: Loss aversion: why losing hurts more than winning feels good
pieces.d: The pain of losing a sum is felt more sharply than the pleasure of gaining the same sum. That imbalance bends decisions about money, work and risk.

pieces.h: Fold equity: winning without the best hand
pieces.d: A bet can win two ways: by being called and holding up, or by making the other player fold. The second way has a value you can estimate.

pieces.h: Tax brackets: why a raise never costs you money
pieces.d: A widespread fear holds that earning more can push you into a higher bracket and leave you with less. With a marginal system, that is not how it works.

pieces.h: The double slit: the experiment that breaks intuition
pieces.d: Send particles one at a time through two openings and they build a pattern only waves can make. Check which opening each used and the pattern vanishes.

pieces.h: Diodes: the one-way valve
pieces.d: A diode lets current through in one direction and blocks it in the other. That simple trick protects, rectifies, regulates and makes light.

pieces.h: Cooking temperatures: the numbers that keep you safe
pieces.d: Colour and time are unreliable guides to whether food is safe. A cheap thermometer and four numbers remove the guesswork.

pieces.h: The availability heuristic: vivid is not the same as likely
pieces.d: We judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. That shortcut serves us well until memory is fed a distorted sample.

pieces.h: Counting combinations: how many ways can they have it
pieces.d: You cannot see their cards, but you can count how many versions of each hand exist. That count is what turns a guess into an estimate.

pieces.h: Reading an income statement
pieces.d: A company's income statement tells the story of a year in a dozen lines. Read from the top down, it shows where the money came from and where each slice went.

pieces.h: How GPS knows where you are
pieces.d: Your phone finds its position by listening to clocks in orbit. It never sends a signal, and the method depends on timing to billionths of a second.

pieces.h: LEDs: what they need and why they die
pieces.d: An LED is easy to light and easy to kill. The difference is one resistor and an understanding of why current, not voltage, is what you control.

pieces.h: How to read a nutrition label
pieces.d: The panel on the back of the packet answers most questions about a food in under a minute, if you know which three lines to read first.

pieces.h: Base rates: start with how often it happens
pieces.d: Before judging a specific case, ask how things usually turn out for cases like it. Ignoring that step produces confident and badly wrong answers.

pieces.h: Variance and bankroll: surviving your own luck
pieces.d: A winning player can lose for weeks. Knowing how wide the swings run, and keeping enough money to ride them, is part of the skill.

pieces.h: The balance sheet: what a company owns and owes
pieces.d: If the income statement is a film of the year, the balance sheet is a photograph of one day. It rests on a single equation that always holds.

pieces.h: How we know the universe had a beginning
pieces.d: The claim that everything began about 13.8 billion years ago rests on three independent lines of evidence that all point the same way.

pieces.h: The transistor as a switch
pieces.d: A small current controlling a large one. This is the idea underneath every relay driver, every logic gate and every processor ever made.

pieces.h: Cleaning chemistry: what works and what must never be mixed
pieces.d: Most household cleaning comes down to four kinds of chemical. Knowing which does what saves money, and knowing what not to combine prevents real harm.

pieces.h: The pre-mortem: finding the failure before it happens
pieces.d: Imagine the project has already failed, then explain why. Ten minutes of this exercise surfaces risks that weeks of planning politely overlook.

pieces.h: Position: the seat is worth more than the cards
pieces.d: Acting last is the single largest structural advantage in hold'em. Good players build their whole strategy around it.

pieces.h: Profit is not cash
pieces.d: Businesses rarely die from lack of profit. They die when the cash runs out. The difference between the two is the most practical idea in accounting.

pieces.h: How vaccines train the immune system
pieces.d: A vaccine is a rehearsal. It shows the body a harmless preview of a germ so that the real thing meets a prepared defence.

pieces.h: MOSFETs: switching real power with almost no effort
pieces.d: The transistor inside nearly every modern device is controlled by voltage, not current. That difference is why it runs cool while switching amps.

pieces.h: Your breaker panel: what it does and what it is telling you
pieces.d: The grey box on the wall is the safety system for every wire in the house. Knowing how to read it and reset it is basic household literacy.

pieces.h: Flow: when hard work stops feeling like work
pieces.d: There is a state in which attention is total, time distorts and difficult things feel effortless. It has known conditions, and you can arrange them.

pieces.h: Starting hands: what you are really choosing
pieces.d: Choosing which hands to play is the first decision and the most frequent. The right answer depends on what kind of hand it is, not just how pretty it looks.

pieces.h: Unit economics: does each sale make money
pieces.d: Before asking whether a company is profitable, ask whether a single customer is. If the answer is no, growth only makes the hole deeper.

pieces.h: The Black Death: the plague that remade Europe
pieces.d: Between 1347 and 1351 a disease killed something like a third to a half of Europe's people. The survivors inherited a different world.

pieces.h: Op-amps: two rules that explain almost everything
pieces.d: The operational amplifier is the universal building block of analog electronics. Two simple rules let you analyse most circuits built around one.

pieces.h: Where your water shuts off, and why to find it today
pieces.d: A burst pipe can release hundreds of litres an hour. The difference between a wet floor and a ruined house is knowing where one valve is.

pieces.h: Pressure and performance: the arousal curve
pieces.d: A little stress sharpens you and a lot of it wrecks you. Where the turning point lies depends on what you are trying to do.

pieces.h: Raise or fold: why limping loses
pieces.d: Just calling the big blind feels cheap and safe. It is the mark of a losing player, and the reasons are structural.

pieces.h: Pricing: the fastest lever a business has
pieces.d: A small change in price moves profit more than an equal change in sales or costs. Most businesses set their prices with far less thought than the number deserves.

pieces.h: Why Rome fell
pieces.d: The western Roman Empire did not collapse on a single day. It came apart over about two centuries, and historians have proposed more than two hundred reasons why.

pieces.h: The multimeter: the one tool to buy first
pieces.d: If you own a single piece of test equipment, this is it. Knowing its four main functions, and its one dangerous mistake, covers most of what you need.

pieces.h: The furnace filter: the cheapest maintenance in the house
pieces.d: A cardboard rectangle protects the most expensive appliance you own. Changing it on time takes two minutes and prevents a surprising number of breakdowns.

pieces.h: Deliberate practice: how skill is actually built
pieces.d: Experience alone does not make people better. A particular kind of effortful practice does, and it is less pleasant and more specific than simply putting in hours.

pieces.h: The 3-bet: reraising before the flop
pieces.d: A reraise before the flop is the strongest ordinary move in the game. Used well, it wins pots immediately and sets up the rest of the hand.

pieces.h: Moats: why some businesses stay profitable
pieces.d: High profits attract competitors, and competition wears profits away. A few companies hold out for decades. What protects them is called a moat.

pieces.h: The Silk Road: the network that joined Eurasia
pieces.d: It was never one road and few travellers crossed all of it. For over fifteen hundred years it carried goods, religions, technologies and diseases across a continent.

pieces.h: Soldering that works the first time
pieces.d: A good solder joint takes three seconds and lasts decades. A bad one looks almost the same. The difference is where you put the heat.

pieces.h: Car maintenance: the short list that matters
pieces.d: Modern cars are far more reliable than their reputation, provided a handful of items are attended to on time. The schedule is in the glovebox.

pieces.h: Second-order thinking: and then what
pieces.d: Every action has consequences, and the consequences have consequences. Asking one more question than everyone else is a cheap way to avoid expensive mistakes.

pieces.h: Defending the big blind
pieces.d: You have already paid for part of the pot. That discount changes which hands you should play, and misjudging it is one of the costliest leaks in the game.

pieces.h: Your walk-away point: the heart of any negotiation
pieces.d: Your power in a negotiation comes from what you will do if no deal is reached. Knowing that precisely matters more than any tactic at the table.

pieces.h: The Industrial Revolution: when growth began
pieces.d: For most of history, living standards barely changed from one century to the next. Then, in Britain around 1760, something started that has not stopped.

pieces.h: Breadboards: building without solder
pieces.d: A plastic block full of holes lets you assemble a circuit in minutes and change it in seconds. Knowing how the holes connect saves hours of confusion.

pieces.h: Tyres: pressure, tread and the codes on the sidewall
pieces.d: Four patches of rubber, each about the size of a hand, are all that connect a car to the road. Five minutes a month keeps them doing their job.

pieces.h: Inversion: solve it backwards
pieces.d: Many problems that resist a direct attack give way when turned around. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, and avoid that.

pieces.h: Stack-to-pot ratio: how deep the hand really is
pieces.d: One number, worked out on the flop, tells you how strong a hand needs to be before you are willing to play for everything.

pieces.h: What a share of stock actually is
pieces.d: A stock is not a ticker symbol or a line on a chart. It is a legal slice of a real business, and that fact explains how it should be valued.

pieces.h: The crash of 1929 and the Great Depression
pieces.d: The stock market collapse of October 1929 is remembered as the start of the Depression. The crash was dramatic, but it was not, by itself, what broke the economy.

pieces.h: How to read a schematic
pieces.d: A schematic is a map of connections, not a picture of a circuit. Once you know the conventions, any diagram becomes readable.

pieces.h: How to jump-start a car safely
pieces.d: A flat battery is the most common breakdown there is. The procedure is simple, and the order of the four connections is the part that matters.

pieces.h: The famous findings that did not hold up
pieces.d: Several of psychology's best-known results have failed when other researchers repeated the experiments. Knowing which ones makes you a better reader of everything else.

pieces.h: Reading the board: wet, dry and who it favours
pieces.d: Three cards land and the hand changes character. Learning to classify a flop quickly tells you who should be betting and how much.

pieces.h: Bonds and interest rates: the seesaw
pieces.d: A bond is a loan you can sell. Its price moves opposite to interest rates, and understanding why takes one example.

pieces.h: The Manhattan Project
pieces.d: In under three years, a secret programme turned a laboratory discovery into a weapon that ended one war and defined the politics of every decade since.

pieces.h: How to read a datasheet
pieces.d: Every part comes with a document that says exactly what it does and what kills it. Knowing which five sections to read turns forty pages into five minutes.

pieces.h: First aid: the first five minutes
pieces.d: In an emergency, a bystander who knows a few simple actions matters more than equipment. These are the ones worth learning, in outline.

pieces.h: The Dunning-Kruger effect: what the study actually found
pieces.d: It is quoted to mean that stupid people think they are clever. The original finding was narrower, more interesting and applies to everyone.

pieces.h: The continuation bet
pieces.d: You raised before the flop and the flop has come. Betting again is the most frequent play in poker, and knowing when not to is where the profit lies.

pieces.h: How banks create money
pieces.d: Most money is not printed by governments. It comes into existence when a bank makes a loan, which sounds like a trick and is simply how the system works.

pieces.h: Thirteen days: the Cuban Missile Crisis
pieces.d: In October 1962 the United States and the Soviet Union came closer to nuclear war than at any other time. It ended through a deal that stayed secret for decades.

pieces.h: The oscilloscope: seeing voltage move
pieces.d: A multimeter tells you a number. An oscilloscope shows you a picture of how that number changes thousands or millions of times a second.

pieces.h: Home fire safety: the plan to make before you need it
pieces.d: Modern furnishings burn fast, and the time to get out of a burning house can be only a couple of minutes. Preparation decides what happens in those minutes.

pieces.h: Hindsight bias: I knew it all along
pieces.d: Once you know how something turned out, you cannot recover how uncertain it looked beforehand. That distortion makes us unfair judges of decisions.

pieces.h: Bet sizing: saying it with chips
pieces.d: How much you bet is as much a part of the play as whether you bet. A few principles cover most situations.

pieces.h: Opportunity cost and sunk cost
pieces.d: Two ideas from economics improve almost any decision. One is about the options you give up. The other is about the money you have already spent.

pieces.h: The computer that landed on the Moon
pieces.d: Apollo's guidance computer had less processing power than a cheap calculator. In the last minutes of the first landing, its design saved the mission.

pieces.h: Debugging a dead circuit
pieces.d: Circuits fail for boring reasons. A fixed order of checks finds most faults in minutes and stops you from changing things at random.

pieces.h: Your back and your desk
pieces.d: Most back pain is not caused by damage and gets better with movement. The best posture is the one you are about to change.

pieces.h: What is up to you: the Stoic test
pieces.d: A teaching from a Roman slave turned philosopher sorts every worry into two piles. Most distress comes from mistaking one pile for the other.

pieces.h: Value betting: getting paid by worse hands
pieces.d: Most of the money in poker is won by betting good hands and being called by slightly worse ones. Missing those bets is an invisible leak.

pieces.h: Supply, demand and elasticity
pieces.d: Prices are not set by sellers alone or by costs alone. They emerge from two forces meeting, and one extra idea explains why some prices swing wildly.

pieces.h: The transistor: the invention inside everything
pieces.d: A small device demonstrated in a New Jersey laboratory in 1947 replaced the vacuum tube and became the most manufactured object in human history.

pieces.h: Batteries: chemistry, capacity and care
pieces.d: A battery is a chemical reaction packaged to deliver electrons on demand. The chemistry inside decides its voltage, its capacity and how it should be treated.

pieces.h: Laundry: the chemistry in the drum
pieces.d: Washing clothes is applied chemistry. Knowing what detergent does and what the symbols on the label mean keeps clothes cleaner and lasting longer.

pieces.h: How to give feedback people can use
pieces.d: Most criticism fails because it is vague, late or aimed at the person. A simple structure makes it specific enough to act on and hard to take as an attack.

pieces.h: The check-raise
pieces.d: Checking and then raising when your opponent bets is the out-of-position player's main weapon. It builds pots, punishes automatic bets and wins hands outright.

pieces.h: Insurance: what is worth insuring and what is not
pieces.d: Insurance loses money on average, by design. It is still one of the most sensible purchases you can make, for the right risks only.

pieces.h: How the internet moves your data
pieces.d: A message crossing the internet is chopped into pieces that travel separately and are reassembled at the far end. No single authority directs any of it.

pieces.h: Logic levels, pull-ups and floating pins
pieces.d: Digital circuits treat voltages as ones and zeros. The rules about where one ends and the other begins explain a whole family of mysterious faults.

pieces.h: Hanging things on walls so they stay there
pieces.d: A shelf or a television that falls off the wall was fixed to the wrong thing. Knowing what is behind the plasterboard is most of the job.

pieces.h: Listening: the half of conversation most people skip
pieces.d: Most of us spend other people's sentences preparing our own. Real listening is a learnable set of behaviours, and it changes what people are willing to tell you.

pieces.h: Bluffing: how often, with what, and against whom
pieces.d: A bluff is a bet with the worst hand that makes a better one fold. Good bluffs are chosen by arithmetic and by the cards you hold, not by nerve.

pieces.h: Dollar-cost averaging: investing on a schedule
pieces.d: Putting in a fixed amount at regular intervals removes the need to choose the right moment. What it achieves, and what it does not, is often misunderstood.

pieces.h: Longitude: the clock that found a ship's position
pieces.d: For centuries sailors could tell how far north or south they were and had no reliable way to know east from west. A carpenter solved it with a watch.

pieces.h: What is inside a microcontroller
pieces.d: A complete computer on one chip, for the price of a coffee. Knowing its parts explains what it can do and why it differs from the processor in a laptop.

pieces.h: The basic toolkit: twelve tools that cover most jobs
pieces.d: Most household repairs need the same few tools. Buying them once, at reasonable quality, costs less than a single call-out fee.

pieces.h: Writing clearly: say the thing
pieces.d: Unclear writing is usually unclear thinking with decoration. A handful of habits make almost anyone easier to read.

pieces.h: Think in ranges, not hands
pieces.d: Trying to guess the exact two cards an opponent holds is a losing habit. Strong players assign a whole set of possible hands and narrow it street by street.

pieces.h: Bubbles: from tulips to dot-coms
pieces.d: Every few decades, the price of something rises far beyond what it can be worth, and then collapses. The stories differ in detail and are alike in structure.

pieces.h: Why the calendar has leap years
pieces.d: The Earth does not circle the Sun in a whole number of days. Twenty centuries of adjustments to cope with that are why February is odd and why 1900 had no leap day.

pieces.h: PWM: faking analog with a fast switch
pieces.d: A digital pin can only be on or off. Switch it quickly enough, and vary how long it stays on, and it can dim a light or set a motor's speed.

pieces.h: Walking: the most underrated exercise
pieces.d: It needs no equipment, skill or membership. The evidence that regular walking lengthens life and improves health is as solid as anything in exercise science.

pieces.h: The river: the last decision
pieces.d: No more cards are coming. Every hand is now exactly one of three things, and knowing which one yours is settles most river decisions.

pieces.h: Analog to digital: how a chip reads the real world
pieces.d: Temperature, light and sound are continuous. A processor only understands numbers. The converter that bridges them has limits worth knowing.

pieces.h: Tilt: the leak that is not about cards
pieces.d: Every player knows how to play better than they do when upset. Managing that gap is worth more than most strategy study.

pieces.h: UART, I2C and SPI: how chips talk
pieces.d: Three simple standards carry nearly all the conversation between a microcontroller and the parts around it. Each makes a different trade between wires, speed and convenience.

pieces.h: Table selection: where you sit matters more than how you play
pieces.d: Your profit comes from the gap between your skill and your opponents'. Choosing whom you play against is the easiest way to widen it.

pieces.h: Debouncing: why one press reads as ten
pieces.d: A mechanical switch does not close cleanly. For a few thousandths of a second it chatters, and a fast chip counts every bounce.

pieces.h: Live tells: what bodies give away, and what they do not
pieces.d: Physical tells are real but far less reliable than films suggest. Betting patterns tell you more, and the best use of tell-reading is to break close decisions.

pieces.h: Voltage regulators: linear or switching
pieces.d: Circuits need a steady voltage and sources rarely provide one. Two families of regulator solve the problem in very different ways.

pieces.h: Tournaments and cash games are different sports
pieces.d: The cards and the rules are identical. The incentives are not, and a strategy that wins in one format can lose steadily in the other.

pieces.h: Decoupling capacitors and ground: the invisible wiring
pieces.d: Many circuits that fail for no apparent reason are missing a few small capacitors or have a careless ground. These dull details decide whether a design is reliable.

pieces.h: The bubble and why chips are not worth what they say
pieces.d: Near the prize money, losing chips hurts more than winning the same number helps. That imbalance has a name and a calculation, and it changes correct play.

pieces.h: The 555 timer: the chip that would not die
pieces.d: Designed in the early 1970s, it is still made by the billion. With two resistors and a capacitor it can blink, beep, delay or debounce.

pieces.h: Short stacks: when to move all in
pieces.d: With ten big blinds, poker reduces to a single decision before the flop. It is the most thoroughly solved part of the game and one of the easiest to learn.

pieces.h: Relays: letting a small circuit switch a big one
pieces.d: A relay is a switch operated by an electromagnet. It lets five volts from a microcontroller control a load on an entirely separate circuit.

pieces.h: Game theory or exploitation: two ways to win
pieces.d: One approach aims to be unbeatable. The other aims to punish specific mistakes. Strong players understand the first well enough to practise the second.

pieces.h: Sensors: how circuits feel the world
pieces.d: Every sensor does the same basic thing: it turns some physical quantity into an electrical one. A handful of principles cover most of those you will meet.

pieces.h: Reviewing your play: where improvement happens
pieces.d: Nobody gets better during the session. Skill is built afterwards, by looking honestly at decisions with the result set aside.

pieces.h: The RC low-pass filter: one resistor, one capacitor
pieces.d: Two cheap parts can strip the fast wiggles off a signal and keep the slow part. One formula tells you where the line between fast and slow falls.

pieces.h: The body clock: light, timing and jet lag
pieces.d: A clock in your brain sets when you feel sleepy and alert, and light is what sets the clock. Knowing when to seek light and when to avoid it fixes more than willpower does.

pieces.h: The default effect: the option nobody chose
pieces.d: Whatever happens when you do nothing is the choice most people end up with. Whoever sets the default has quietly made the decision for the majority.

pieces.h: APR and APY: two ways to quote one rate
pieces.d: Lenders quote the rate that looks smaller and savings accounts quote the one that looks bigger. Both are honest. Here is how to convert between them.

pieces.h: Flopping a set: the odds behind set mining
pieces.d: A small pocket pair is mostly a ticket to hit three of a kind. Here is how often that happens and how deep the stacks must be for the ticket to pay.

pieces.h: The shipping container: the box that shrank the world
pieces.d: A steel box with standard corners cut the cost of loading a ship so far that distance almost stopped mattering to trade.

pieces.h: The comparator: deciding between two voltages
pieces.d: A comparator answers one question: which of two voltages is higher. Add one resistor for hysteresis and it stops dithering when the answer is close.

pieces.h: Salt: when to add it and why
pieces.d: Salt does more than make food salty. Added at the right moment, it changes how food holds water, how it browns and how every other flavour comes across.

pieces.h: Survivorship bias: the evidence that did not come back
pieces.d: We study the winners because they are the ones still around to study. The failures that would complete the picture have dropped out of sight.

pieces.h: Fees: the one percent that takes a quarter
pieces.d: An annual fee of one percent sounds like almost nothing. Over thirty years it takes roughly a quarter of what you would otherwise have had.

pieces.h: What the flop gives you: the odds of hitting
pieces.d: Most hands miss most flops. Knowing the real frequencies of pairs, draws and overcards stops you from expecting help that is not coming.

pieces.h: 1453: the fall of Constantinople
pieces.d: For a thousand years a triple wall kept every army out of Constantinople. In the spring of 1453 a young sultan broke it with the largest guns yet built.

pieces.h: The LM317: one rule, any voltage
pieces.d: The LM317 adjustable regulator has been on benches since the 1970s. It does one thing, holding 1.25 volts between two of its pins, and everything else follows from that.

pieces.h: Eggs: what heat does to them
pieces.d: An egg goes from liquid to solid over a span of about twenty degrees. Knowing which part sets at which temperature explains every way of cooking one.

pieces.h: The memory palace: remembering with places
pieces.d: Your memory for places is far stronger than your memory for lists. A technique more than two thousand years old lets you store one in the other.

pieces.h: The cash flow statement: where the money went
pieces.d: The income statement says whether a company made a profit. The cash flow statement says whether it got any money, and what it did with it.

pieces.h: Stealing the blinds: the arithmetic of the button raise
pieces.d: When everyone folds to you in late position, the blinds are money lying on the table. A short sum shows how often a raise has to work, and what changes the answer.

pieces.h: Marie Curie in five minutes
pieces.d: She coined the word radioactivity, found two elements in a shed, and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

pieces.h: The thermistor: temperature from a divider
pieces.d: A thermistor is a resistor that changes with temperature. One fixed resistor and an analog input turn it into a thermometer good to a fraction of a degree.

pieces.h: The water heater: the tank in the cupboard
pieces.d: A storage water heater is a simple machine with two safety parts that matter a great deal. Ten minutes of attention a year extends its life.

pieces.h: Regression to the mean: why streaks fade
pieces.d: An extreme result is usually followed by a more ordinary one, with no cause at all. Missing this leads people to credit cures, punishments and jinxes that did nothing.

pieces.h: How an insurer makes money: underwriting and float
pieces.d: An insurance company can pay out almost everything it collects and still do well. It earns from two sources, and the second is holding other people's money.

pieces.h: Paired boards: when the flop shows a pair
pieces.d: A flop such as king, seven, seven is hard for anyone to hit. That single fact decides who should bet, how much, and when to believe a raise.

pieces.h: Why the Moon always shows the same face
pieces.d: The Moon spins exactly once for each trip around the Earth. That is no coincidence. Gravity slowed it until the two motions matched.

pieces.h: Driving a DC motor: from one transistor to the H-bridge
pieces.d: A motor needs far more current than a logic pin can give, and it fights back when switched off. Here is the safe way to run one forwards, backwards and at any speed.
pieces.s: Motors and how to drive them

pieces.h: Fixing a running toilet
pieces.d: A toilet that hisses or refills by itself is wasting water around the clock. The cause is nearly always one of two cheap parts in the tank.

pieces.h: How to apologise so it lands
pieces.d: A good apology repairs trust and a bad one makes things worse. The difference lies in a few parts that can be learned, and in a few words to leave out.

pieces.h: Concessions: how to give ground without losing it
pieces.d: Every negotiation involves moving from where you started. How you move, and what you ask for each time you do, shapes the deal as much as where you began.

pieces.h: ICM by hand: working one example
pieces.d: The independent chip model turns tournament stacks into money. Doing the sum once, with three players, makes clear why a coin flip for your stack is a bad bet near the prizes.

pieces.h: The birthday problem: why coincidences are common
pieces.d: In a group of only 23 people, two of them more likely than not share a birthday. The reason is that you are counting pairs, not people.

pieces.h: How a touchscreen finds your finger
pieces.d: A phone screen does not feel pressure. It measures hundreds of tiny capacitors many times a second and notices which ones your finger has disturbed.

pieces.h: Changing a flat tyre safely
pieces.d: The job takes fifteen minutes with the tools already in the car. Most of the danger comes from where you stop and from the jack, so those come first.

pieces.h: Occam's razor: the simplest explanation that fits
pieces.d: When several explanations fit the facts, start with the one that assumes the least. It is a rule for where to look first, not a guarantee of where the truth lies.

pieces.h: Comparative advantage: why trade pays even for the best at everything
pieces.d: A country, a company or a person can be better at every task and still gain by handing some of them over. The reason is opportunity cost, and one example shows it.

pieces.h: Minimum defence frequency: how often you must not fold
pieces.d: If you fold too often to a bet, any two cards become a profitable bluff against you. One fraction tells you where that line sits for every bet size.

pieces.h: How we know the age of the Earth
pieces.d: The figure of 4.54 billion years comes from measuring atoms in meteorites. Getting there took a century of argument and one of the first ultra-clean laboratories.

pieces.h: From gates to an adder
pieces.d: Every calculation a computer makes comes down to adding binary digits with a handful of logic gates. You can follow the whole circuit in five minutes.

pieces.h: The golden mean: Aristotle on virtue as a skill
pieces.d: Aristotle held that good character lies between two ways of going wrong and is built by practice, like a craft. His account still works as a method.

pieces.h: Roth or traditional: when to pay the tax
pieces.d: American retirement accounts come in two tax flavours. The choice between them rests on one comparison, your tax rate now against your tax rate later.

pieces.h: Roulette: one number that never changes
pieces.d: Every spin of a roulette wheel carries the same built-in loss, whatever you bet on and however you stagger your stakes. The sum takes one line.
